coordinates.locator: Position walked along the OSM Jinping traffic-tunnel line by the sourced portal-to-hall distance (see geometry:cjpl-i-point method)
coordinates.note: The position is derived along an OpenStreetMap trace of the Jinping traffic tunnel from the distance to the CJPL-I hall published in an arXiv paper. Neither is a surveyed hall position, so the point is shown as campus-grade and approximate. It replaces an earlier geocoder point of 2 km precision (28.1763431, 101.720304).

depth_mwe.note: 2400 m of vertical rock times a measured average density of 2.8 g/cm^3. This replaces an earlier "~2400 m.w.e.", which repeated the rock thickness in metres as a water-equivalent depth; the 2014 CJPL-II paper (arXiv:1404.2651) it was credited to states 6,720 m. Woodley et al. 2024 infer an effective flat-overburden depth of 6.20 ± 0.13 km.w.e. from the measured flux instead.
depth_mwe.quote: The water equivalent depth of CJPL is calculated to be 6720m as the product of the measured average rock density of 2.8g/cm3 and the depth of 2400m.

muon_flux.locator: Abstract and Sec. 6, Chin. Phys. C 45, 025001 (arXiv:2007.15925)
muon_flux.note: Jinping Neutrino Experiment 1-ton liquid-scintillator prototype in CJPL-I: 264 muon events in 645.2 days with reconstructed directions; the 2025 CJPL-II paper calls it the efficiency-corrected CJPL-I flux. Its vertical intensity, (2.0 ± 0.3 stat.) × 10^-10 cm^-2 s^-1 sr^-1, is not a flux and is not recorded. The earlier plastic-scintillator telescope result, (2.0 ± 0.4) × 10^-10 cm^-2 s^-1 or 61.7 ± 11.7 per m^2 per year (Wu et al. 2013), had no angular correction to the detector acceptance, which is why the JNE value is used here; the 2018 CJPL review (Table I) still tabulates it as 0.17 per m^2 per day. Woodley et al. 2024 Table III lists JNE as (3.53 ± 0.29) × 10^-10. The quote's factor 10^-10 multiplies the whole bracket, so the stored value is 3.53 × 10^-10 cm^-2 s^-1 with no unit conversion.
muon_flux.quote: measured the cosmic-ray muon flux to be (3.53 ± 0.22stat. ± 0.07sys. ) × 10−10 cm−2 s−1

name: CJPL-I

summary.plain: The original hall of the China Jinping Underground Laboratory, reached from a hydropower station tunnel under more than two kilometres of mountain rock in Sichuan, China.
summary.technical: CJPL-I: the original CJPL hall beside the Jinping traffic tunnel, Sichuan, inaugurated 2010, with ~2400 m of rock overburden (~6720 m.w.e.), among the deepest overburdens of any underground laboratory in the world.
